2102368970602959173.text:
One of our clients grew their agency revenue by roughly 500% in 12 months.

Here's the exact LinkedIn funnel we built to help them do it:

1. Content → Attention

We built the content around the problems their ideal brands were already trying to solve, so every post had a job: build authority, expose a problem, show proof, handle an objection or push someone further into the funnel.

2. Lead Magnets → Demand Capture

We created resources around specific problems their ICP wanted solved immediately.

One of the first ones took off and generated roughly 30-40 calls by itself.

The important part was that the resources were directly connected to what they sold, so the people downloading them were potential buyers, not random LinkedIn users.

3. Opt-In Pages → Owned Audience

Rather than giving every resource away directly in the DMs, we started sending traffic through dedicated opt-in pages.

Name + email → resource delivered → prospect added to the database.

Now a LinkedIn post wasn't valuable for 48 hours and every successful post permanently grew an audience they could market to again.

4. VSLs → Pre-Selling

We built VSL pages between the content and the sales call.

They explained the problem, their methodology, who the service was for, relevant proof and why someone should work with them.

By the time someone booked, they'd already consumed 10-20 minutes of sales material.

5. DMs → Conversion

Every comment, connection and high-intent interaction became an opportunity to start a conversation.

Instead of immediately pitching, the goal was to identify intent, understand their situation and move qualified prospects toward a call.

6. Email → Nurture

Most people aren't going to buy the week they discover you.

So the email database became the second layer of the funnel, continuously putting case studies, insights, offers and proof in front of prospects who weren't ready the first time.

7. Qualification → Better Calls

Eventually we actually started optimizing for fewer calls.

We tightened the messaging around larger brands, made the funnel do more of the education and filtered out companies that weren't a fit.

Call volume came down, but the average quality went up significantly.

8. Distribution → Compounding Growth

One founder profile went from roughly 10,000 to 64,000 followers and generated around 5M impressions in 12 months.

That meant every new post, lead magnet, case study and offer was being launched into a progressively larger pool of potential buyers.

He managed to achieve roughly 400-500% revenue growth in 12 months.

The bigger opportunity is building the infrastructure behind the content so every impression has somewhere to go.

If you're a founder or running GTM, build one account list your whole growth engine can use.

Start with your 10 best customers. Put their domains into AI Ark's lookalike search, find similar companies, and pull 2 to 3 buyers per account. Verify their emails and fill the gaps with Prospeo.

Keep the company domain, segment, buying trigger, outreach tier and status together in Clay. That record should tell the next tool who the account is and what's already happened.

Then build the campaign around it:

→ Outbound: tier accounts by segment fit and a live buying trigger. Accounts with both get email, LinkedIn and a call from your team. Those with either one get email and LinkedIn. Keep broader-fit accounts with neither on email.

→ Paid: use the company list for LinkedIn ads and Vibe’s streaming TV ads. Match the data to each platform's requirements. Google Customer Match needs first-party contacts. Keep the offer consistent as you adapt the creative.

→ Search and landing pages: answer the questions buyers ask about pricing, alternatives and how the work gets done. Give each segment a page with a clear promise, proof and next action. Use the same brief for the page, ads and outreach.

→ Workflows: build a workflow that connects reply events across your tools. When someone responds, have it stop their other sequences, update the CRM and write the result back to the account. Add a monthly refresh to re-verify emails and update the tiers.

→ Reporting: bring matched ad exposure, tracked site activity and CRM deals into an account-level view. Compare results by segment. Use what you find to choose the next audience, page or follow-up to improve.

Before launching, prepare and warm up your sending domains, install page tracking and check that the audiences are ready. Get one segment working before adding more channels.

At Frontal, Ivan runs paid media that used to take 6 people. Connecting the work is a big part of the job now.

my business partner is not going to like this:

we have a cold-email playbook that uses a specific site with ~6,779 B2B categories + over 1M case studies sitting on it lol.

here it is kids: casestudies(.)com/categories

this is basically an infinite demand gen playbook if u know how to read it.

heres exactly how:

1. use the category page as the market map
dont sit there scrolling around looking for the coolest software.

youre looking for categories where:

- 1 new customer could easily be worth $20K+
- companies can reasonably buy inside 3-4 weeks
- the buyer is easy to identify + reach
- vendors already have multiple public case studies
- the result is repeatable across lots of similar companies
- the demand gen work can be fulfilled without praying for miracles

important: these are hypotheses at first. u do not know a company's ACV or sales cycle just because AI guessed from a category name.

2. turn the categories into a scoring queue

have Codex or Claude structure the markets u want to inspect, then use Jev to score each one across the same closed set of questions:

- likely ACV band
- likely sales cycle band
- size of the reachable buyer universe
- how obvious the economic outcome is
- how much public proof exists
- how easy the delivery would be
- how confident the overall fit is

Jev gives u the order to research and index them.

it doesnt turn a guess into a fact.

manually validate the top markets before u build anything.

3. open a category, then open 1 company inside it

go directly to the company's own website + case studies.

use the directory for discovery. dont clone their database or mirror a million PDFs into some commercial warehouse. keep the source URL, follow the site's terms + warehouse YOUR research and scoring.

find a company with a few strong case studies and pull:

- customer name + domain
- what type of business they are
- size, location + operating model
- the problem they had
- the outcome they got
- why they were a fit
- who likely owned the buying decision
- any trigger that made the timing make sense

4. pick the most repeatable case study

not always the biggest logo.

pick the customer where u can explain exactly why another X amount of companies would have the same problem + want the same outcome.

that company becomes the seed.

5. run the seed domain through DiscoLike

give it:

- the case study customer's domain
- a plain english description of the ICP
- company size
- geography
- business model
- industry
- any tech, growth or operating signal that actually mattered in the case study

pull a few dozen lookalikes, then review the list.
similar does not automatically mean qualified.

every company still needs a reason to be there.

6. send this email to the company that published the case study

subject: {{firstName}} {{casestudy_companyname}}?

“{{firstName}} - we took the {{caseStudyCompany}} case study from your site and mapped a few thousand companies that look extremely similar to them.

same offers, sizes and signals that made {{caseStudyCompany}} a fit for {{caseStudyOutcome}}.

want me to send over the first 20?”

thats it.

youre using proof THEY already trust to show them where the next version of that customer could come from.

the part most people will fuck up comes after they reply yes.

7. do the work immediately

run the final DiscoLike search through the app, API or MCP, then manually review 10-20 companies before sending anything.

reply with the sample directly inside the email:

- company
- domain
- 1 line on why it looks like the case study customer

dont attach a giant mystery CSV full of shit u havent checked.

give them the useful part right there, then add 2 real meeting times + your calendar.

8. understand what u optimized for

that first email is optimized for a positive reply.

it is NOT optimized for a booked call.

so once they raise their hand, u need to be way more aggressive about converting the interest.

if they dont book, call them the next day.

“hey {{firstName}}, calling about the {{number}} companies I sent over from the {{caseStudyCompany}} case study. did u get a chance to look through them?”

now the call isnt cold anymore.

ur following up on completed work they asked u to send.

9. expand the sample into the actual engagement
on the call, show them what this looks like across every useful case study they have:

- use each successful customer as a seed
- map the lookalike market around each one
- combine + dedupe the full TAM
- find the right decision makers
- build the outbound campaigns
- agree on the exact buy box
- generate meetings
- let the client approve which ones are genuinely worth pursuing

now ur not selling a random lead list.

ur selling a defined number of qualified, pursuable opportunities built around customers they already know they can help.

and this is where the $20K+ engagement can make sense IF their customer economics, market size, sales cycle + ability to fulfil it support the price.

10. save the play so it compounds

for every market, store:

- category
- company being targeted
- case study URL
- seed customer + domain
- case study outcome
- lookalike filters
- estimated ACV band
- estimated sales cycle band
- Jev score + confidence
- sample sent
- positive reply
- meeting booked
- opportunity accepted
- rejection reason

after a while u dont have a folder of random lead magnets.

u have an indexed bank of markets, proof, offers, seed customers, lookalike searches, copy + actual response data.

the company already told the internet who they can help + what they did for them.

ur job is to find more companies that look like that customer, hand them the first 20 + ask if they want u to build the machine that keeps doing it.

hell of a lot easier to buy than “we do lead gen.”

2103122787221299674.text:
If I inherited a B2B company doing $5M a year with 4 reps & no outbound motion, here's exactly what I'd build in the first 90 days:

(We've run this build for 100+ B2B companies & it's the same sequence every time)

Step 1: Pull the last 20 sales calls before touching a tool

Nobody gets to buy a domain until this is done.

> the last 20 recorded sales calls
> the last 10 closed-won accounts
> the last 10 closed-lost, with the reason

Read the transcripts for the pain that repeats, in the prospect's own words.

Not "pipeline problems." The actual phrase they used.

Then look at what was observably true about the closed-won accounts before they bought.

> a role they were hiring for
> a tool they'd just added
> a complaint pattern in their reviews.

That becomes the scoring rubric for the entire market.

The output is a persona written as a situation.

"VP Sales" is everyone with the title. "VP who inherited 8 reps on a 2019 stack" is 400 people with the same problem this quarter.

Write the disqualifiers with the same care. Without them the model invents reasons a company qualifies.

Prompt I'd feed Claude with the transcripts attached:

"Read these 20 call transcripts & 10 closed-won account summaries. Return: the 3 pain points that appear most, quoted in the prospect's words. The observable signals that were true before each closed-won account bought. 3 personas written as situations rather than titles. A list of hard disqualifiers. Return none where nothing is found. Never invent a signal."

Step 2: Map the whole market, not a list

A list is 2,000 contacts someone hand-picked. A market is every account that could ever buy, scored.

Apollo's free account gives a rough count.

Plug in the filters, read the number, multiply by 0.7 for what survives verification.

Under 10,000 contacts, this is an ABM motion & everything below is manual.

10,000 to 100,000 is where the machine makes sense.

Past 100,000 you're leaving money on the table every month you don't run it.

Score every account on timing signals, weighted:

> hiring for the role you replace: 10 points
> raised in the last 12 months: 10 points
> new exec in the seat you sell to: 10 points
> complaint pattern in reviews: 10 points
> running paid ads: 6 points
> tech on the stack that pairs with yours: 5 points

An account carrying 3 of those is worth several times the effort of one carrying none.

Re-score every 90 days. A funding round from 14 months ago says nothing about this quarter's budget.

Step 3: Be honest about the offer

(This decides more than anything else below & it's the step everyone skips)

The offer decides which band you land in:

> blue ocean, nothing like it: 1 lead per 25 to 200 contacts
> real product market fit: 1 per 200 to 500
> crowded category: 1 per 500 to 1,000
> SEO, security, recruiting: 1 per 1,000 to 10,000

That's a 400x swing on one variable.

Then build the front-end offer.

What goes in the email is something a stranger can say yes to with nothing at stake.

3 kinds that work:

> a sales asset: a case study deck, a playbook, a demo video
> a front-end service: a free campaign, a $500 build, a 30 day pilot
> a free sample: 5 contacts already searching for them, handed over

3 kinds that don't work:

> a free 20 step audit from a stranger
> "we can replace your entire marketing team"
> "your current system is broken, let us rip it out"

The test is whether the prospect loses anything by saying yes.

If the answer is time, trust or a meeting, it's NOT a front-end offer.

Step 4: Buy the infrastructure on day one

Because it needs 3 weeks before a single cold email sends, & everything above happens in parallel while it warms.

> domains from Porkbun, .com only, no hyphens or numbers
> inboxes from ScaledMail, they set up DNS & swap burned accounts
> Google: 2 to 3 inboxes per domain, 15 cold sends each per day
> Microsoft Azure: 25 to 49 per domain, 2 to 3 sends each

Warmup runs 14 to 21 days. Start at 5 warm emails a day, add one a day until you're at 20. Leave it running forever.

Then a ramp.

Nobody goes from zero cold sends to 15. Start at 5, add one a day, watch the reply rate. If it dips when you step up, step back.

Campaign settings that are never negotiable:

> plain text, no HTML
> no open tracking pixel, it hurts placement
> no unsubscribe link, a spintax opt-out keyword instead
> 8am to 5pm EST, weekdays
> one follow-up, 3 days later, then a new campaign

And pull the MX record for every contact before sending.

Google & Microsoft filter differently enough that the two halves reply at rates that aren't close.

Run them as separate campaigns.

Step 5: Build the list while the inboxes warm

3 sources, in order of how much everyone else is using them:

> Google Maps, one zip code at a time, for anything local
> trade directories & certification bodies for niche verticals
> Apollo via a scraper, for the general B2B core

Google Maps is the one nobody runs properly.

There are 32,000 zip codes in the US & pulling one at a time means every query returns something.

Local businesses live there, not on LinkedIn.

Directories are where the odd data lives.

One client wanted architecture firms certified by a specific body.

The body publishes a member list. Instant Data Scraper pulled the whole thing in an afternoon.

Then qualify before you enrich.

Run every company's website through an AI column with the ICP & disqualifiers from step 1.

Raw scraping lands 50 to 60% ICP fit.

Qualifying first lands 90 to 95%, and you stop paying credits on companies you were always going to drop.

Then the waterfall:

> Icypeas first, cheapest
> Prospeo & LeadMagic for whatever's left
> LeadMagic to verify every result

Roughly 70% of a raw pull survives all of that.

For local markets, scrape the public addresses too.

On one build we ran for a client: the paid route found 3,621 contacts and their own websites found 4,553 more.

The paid ones took 94.94 contacts per positive reply. The public ones took 54.97.

Step 6: Write 15 variants, not one

The rules every script follows:

> under 65 words, ideally under 45
> subject line 1 to 3 words, lowercase, relevant
> written like you're messaging a coworker
> spintax on every sentence, or the filters fingerprint you
> a soft CTA, never "got 15 minutes?"
> social proof only from the same industry, or none

Then the frameworks. (These are the ones that have held across every vertical)

The one-liner free offer:

"Hey Sarah, interested in a free cold email campaign where we target 10,000 of your ICP prospects for Acme?"

One of the best performing emails we've ever sent. The whole thing rides on the offer being a no-brainer.

Lead magnet plus case study:

"Hey John, created a TikTok Shop playbook for Acme outlining what we used to take a client from $0 to $200k/month in 90 days. Mind if I send it over?"

Pain point plus solution:

"Hi Tyler, how are your crews handling roof inspections, phone in one hand & clipboard in the other? We built smart glasses that capture photos & checklists hands-free while they're on the roof. Mind if I share how they work?"

That roofing email did phenomenally, because nobody had ever named that specific pain to a roofer before.

Write 15 to 30 of these. Launch all of them at once.

Step 7: Launch & give every variant 1,000 sends

Nobody's allowed an opinion on a script before it's had 1,000 sends.

After 2 weeks, kill the bottom two thirds & put every send behind what's left.

We've had campaigns where one of four variants was producing every lead.

Removing the other three TRIPLED results overnight, and it was only visible because someone checked.

What the numbers mean in the first month:

> reply rate under 0.5%: deliverability problem, stop & diagnose
> reply rate dropped overnight: copy fatigue or a burned domain
> bounce rate over 3%: pull the list
> zero replies & zero bounces: the emails never left, copy's shadow-banned

Step 8: Add the phone in week 3

This is the layer that separates a campaign from a system.

> a parallel dialer, Salesfinity
> callers hired & trained for 2 weeks before a dial
> 500 dials a day per caller
> every positive email reply called the same day

On our recent build for a landscaping SaaS, 41,150 emails booked 20 meetings & 32,577 dials booked 33.

The phone produced 62% of the meetings off 44% of the touchpoints.

Every one of those dials was into a phone that hadn't rung with a real person in weeks, because everyone else moved to email years ago.

9.2% connect rate is the benchmark. Under that, the list is wrong.

Step 9: Score every reply the day it lands

This is where cost per meeting gets decided & it's the layer that never gets built.

The system:

> EmailBison fires a webhook on every reply
> n8n classifies intent: interested, more info, wrong person, cost, out of office
> the reply lands in Slack with full context & the prospect's number
> a rep responds inside 5 minutes

After 20 minutes, meeting conversion drops 50 to 80%. That's the whole reason for the automation.

Then tier them.

Score every reply against your own rubric as a percentage:

> 90 to 100: senior rep, account research attached
> 75 to 90: rep, personalised sequence
> 50 to 75: automated cadence
> under 50: flagged in Slack, never binned

Templates for the 5 replies you'll get. Never type them fresh.

Interested: "Thanks Sarah, here's a bit more context on what this looks like for Acme. Free Tuesday at 2pm EST?"

Cost: "Pricing varies but we typically run a monthly retainer. Can't give exact numbers since it depends on scope. Happy to talk for 7 minutes about it if you're open to it, if not no worries."

That second one pulls back more skeptical people than anything else we've written.

Step 10: Protect the meeting

Cold outbound meetings show at 30 to 50% with nothing in place. This gets them above 75%.

> confirmation email with a 60 second video of who they'll meet
> a longer video or one-pager to watch before
> reminders at 24 hours, 4 hours, 1 hour, 10 minutes
> a LinkedIn connection request the day they book
> a call from the rep before the meeting if there's a number

Book them inside 2 days. A meeting 2 weeks out is a meeting they'll forget.

Step 11: Optimise on the right number

Reply rate is a deliverability signal. It is not a performance metric.

The number that matters is contact-to-lead ratio. How many people do you contact to produce one interested reply.

> 300 to 1 is strong
> 500 to 1 is solid
> past 1,500 to 1, the offer or the market is the problem

Split it by segment every week.

One or two segments carry almost everything & the average hides which.

Re-enrich the whole list monthly. 30 to 50% of it has moved or changed inside 6 months.

Step 12: SCALE

The volume formula: total verified TAM, divided by 3 months, multiplied by emails per sequence. That's your monthly send.

The goal is every account in the market contacted once every 90 days across email, phone & LinkedIn.

Then the list re-scores, the winning angle rotates, and the next pass starts.

What 90 days looks like when it's done in this order:

> a foodservice manufacturer: 1,061 leads in 70 days at 100k emails a month
> a landscaping SaaS: 53 meetings in the first 50 days from zero
> a financial services firm: 31 interested replies, $4M in pipeline

None of those 3 companies changed their product, reps or pricing.

The order changed. That's the whole build.

P.S. If you'd rather have this built & run for you, DM me "GTM" & I'll walk you through what it looks like on your market.

I've watched cold email agencies charge $5k/mo to send 20k-40k cold emails per month

Here's where that money actually goes.

(most of it isn't what you think)

A real month of a $5k retainer is ~40 hours of work. I broke it down:

List building + scraping — ~10 hrs
Enrichment + verifying data — ~6 hrs
Writing + rewriting copy — ~6 hrs
Sequence setup + sending — ~4 hrs
Inbox monitoring + sorting replies — ~6 hrs
Strategy: offer, targeting, angle — ~4 hrs
Reporting + client comms — ~2 hrs

Now look at that list again.

Of 40 hours, ~6 need a human. The strategy (4) and the live-reply judgment (2).

The other 34 are process. And in 2026, process is free (hint: Claude follows SOPs better than VAs)

Here's what each line item costs you now instead of a retainer:

List building → Clay/Deepline search + AI enrichment
Enrichment → one prompt on a raw CSV
Copywriting → a messaging framework (below)
Sending → any LinkedIn/email automation tool
Reply sorting → AI drafts, you approve

The 3 things that still need YOU:

The offer. What you sell, to whom, why they care. No tool invents your wedge.

The targeting call. Which segment, which trigger, which list is worth the send.

Live reply judgment. When a real prospect writes back, a human decides the move.

Everything else is a solved problem.

The messaging framework I used to watch top operators guard like a secret:

One idea per message.

If it needs two, it's two messages.

Relevance > personalization.

Right segment beats clever first line.

Open a conversation, don't pitch.

First message earns a reply, nothing more.

Sixth-grade english.

Short words, no polish that screams template.

Run every draft against those 4 before it sends. That's the whole thing.

You were never paying $5k for effort.

You were paying for judgment wrapped in 34 hours of process.

A business plan that assumes the best-case scenario for every variable is not a strategy. It is a wish list with a spreadsheet attached.

AI makes this worse, not better. Ask any model to help you build a 2027 revenue plan and it will give you a clean one. Projected ARR, hiring timeline, CAC, conversion rates, churn assumptions. The numbers connect. The formatting looks credible. The model does not stop to ask whether demand will behave that way, whether pricing will hold, whether you can hire fast enough, or whether the cash position survives a slower ramp.

It generates the forecast you described. It does not challenge the forecast you built.

This is the actual problem with AI-assisted planning right now. The output looks finished because the model is good at producing structured, coherent documents. That coherence can make a plan feel more defensible than it is. You walk into a board meeting or a pitch with numbers that were never pressure-tested from a different angle.

What marketers and operators actually need before committing to a plan is something closer to an opponent. Someone asking: what happens if conversion comes in at 60% of the target? What does churn look like if the product takes longer to earn trust than the model assumed? What does the hiring timeline do to margins if recruiting drags by two quarters?

Those questions do not come from asking one AI model to be more critical. They come from running the plan through multiple models that approach it from different starting assumptions. One model tests the growth case. Another works through the downside. A third looks at operating constraints and cash dependencies. When the models disagree, the disagreement tells you exactly where the plan is fragile.

That is what @agnt_hub is built for. One question, multiple AI perspectives, visible consensus and conflict, and a synthesis that reflects what actually survived the debate.

Before you present a 2027 plan as a position you can defend, run it through a real debate first.

Try it here: https://t.co/jA7VO26lpC

"My friend David Perell told me, 'My Twitter account is more valuable to me than my college education. My Twitter has given me more value to my career and also personally.'"

"College is a bundle of education, network, and credential. You learn from having conversations. You meet people and discover people. It's proof of work: Are they interesting? Are they funny? Did they build something cool?"

"What's more impressive to you: someone who went to Stanford, or someone who is followed by Patrick Collison, Elon Musk, Marc Andreessen, et cetera? I think most people would say the latter. It's this kind of peer-to-peer credential."

"Implicitly, although people often do this explicitly, that is a cosign. It's an endorsement that this person is worth tracking. It's a public signal that this person is worth following."

"If you're followed by these people, now your doors are open. People want to read what you say. They want to work with you. They want to invest in you or have you as part of their team."

"There's benefit to the receiver but there's also benefit to the giver because if you're the first person to discover someone, that's how Silicon Valley operates."

2102996055415488521.text:
Day 15 of writing ancient sales letters by hand to become a skilled copywriter.

I woke up at 4am this morning with my heart beating through my chest as I struggled to breathe.

Momentum has been building. Things have been going well.

But I am overwhelmed.

Trying to learn my new creative strategist role.

With a lot of help from my stepbrother who is also learning with me now.

He’s a killer.

I don’t know of another freak who would get into this…

…and then proceed to read several advertising books cover to cover.

All in one day.

Pushes me to do better.

I’m learning a lot all at once.

Which is good, and I’m adapting to it.

But my body started to freak out a little bit.

And furthermore, my past began to beckon at my door.

It genuinely felt like my old identity was knocking.

Chilling stuff.

I haven’t had a panic attack in a while, but I have had so many that I know exactly what to do.

Waking up I was rather scared, but I instantly began to fix my breathing.

Drank some ice water.

Calmed myself down. Went back to bed.

Unfortunately, I missed my morning QnA call so that I could get some good sleep afterwards.

But I think it was for the best.

Normally, I am all sunshine and rainbows.

Today was just not one of those days.

But today I still had things to do, I struggled with them, but I executed.

Tomorrow will be better for it.

I know that the only real thing that will separate me from anyone else in regard to everything that I am doing…

…is that I started my journey.

Without the intention of ever stopping. 

And I won’t.

That’s really the best variable anyone can have.

The breakdown today will purposefully be of a smaller advertisement.

And I’m actually tired for once. 

Yesterday I had too much energy and I didn’t work out enough.

Leading to panic at 4am.

By the time I sleep tonight though I will have used everything that I have in me.

I need better focus, and I need to prioritize important inputs earlier in my day.

My thoughts are scattered but I will walk through the fog.

I will drill into the wall before me, as it is my future.

Drilling is all I can do.

Thank you for reading today.

This is an important day for me because it was really difficult.

And I began to be cruel to myself today.

Very much fighting myself within my own mind.

But then I remembered what brought me into this state of high energy.

Truly loving myself and I mean it.

(Loving myself doesn't mean always giving in to myself and my whims or my wants).

Then in turn being able to share and give love to others.

It can be hard to do both but to have one you must have the other.

These are the days that matter the most.

A rep is a rep.

I apologize for my lack of full effort.

And I will do better tomorrow.

I suppose these swipe-files are for days like this.

Here is my VERY short breakdown.

Sales letter:

A collection of three print ads that all say “Don’t.”

This was advertised by a few different sources.

Swiped by Mike Schauer.

It ran in the 1860s-1880s roughly.

They all sell different things.

This format is still very much used today.

Reverse psychology is nothing new ha-ha.

This is our oldest example yet.

Key takeaways and learnings: 

Ok, people’s expectations for an ad revolve around the understanding that they want you to buy.

So, when you put “Don’t” at the start of an ad people stop.

And read out of curiosity.

In their mind at first they may assume that the advertisement is saying not to buy the product.

But of course, that brings some confusion.

So, they read on.

It also lowers one's guard, as the messaging sounds like a warning.

Someone trying to help you urgently.

With this first little ad, it almost feels like a short poem at the start.

It begins with a very simple, “DON’T DO IT.”

Which would honestly catch my eyes now but in the late 19th century this would surely stand out.

I’m sure this was relatively novel at the time.

But one can imagine these were printed like crazy after several began to do well.

I guess they would check by giving a little post purchase survey.

Face to face in the shop of course.

The next four lines create confusion; they are telling me not to buy all of these things?

Why?

Followed by:

“In fac, don’t buy anything for yourself or boy until you have seen our stock.”

Before they can think “Ohhh, this makes sense”, they see a big question.

AND WHY?

Well shoot, that's what they were probably thinking of asking already.

“Because we have anything you wish.”

Ok, that’s a COLD ass line.

“The stock is the largest, the styles the best and prices as low as can be found anywhere.

Here they are really competing on their wide selection over anything else.

Not really pushing any sales but they say as low as anywhere else.

And if that is the case, why go somewhere with a much smaller collection?

I believe the don’t mechanism is more so a hook than anything else.

But it’s very cool to see this kind of messaging in an advertisement so old.

The next one is a long slew of don’t, over and over again.

“DON’T BUY A COOK.”

“Stove for wood or coal.”

And then just don’t…after don’t…after don’t…

All in regard to what can only be described as “kitchen appliances” at the time.

They do a very similar format to the first ad, but it’s much more repetitive.

This whole damn advertisement is this mechanism.

Just hammering it in for full effect until the last sentence.

“Before calling on or writing to.”

“E.W. MARKHAM.”

The “Look at cheap column” feels like a way of hinting at how cheap they are which can of course be a good thing depending on who you are targeting.

This suspicion builds when I read “Won’t be undersold.”

As it sounds like they are competing on being the cheapest.

The last ad is SUPER short.

Very sweet and to the point.

Calling out the ladies.

“Ladies, Don’t Buy Until You have seen…”

“Sheman’s New Patent.”

“AS-YOU-LIKE-IT SKIRT.”

Just selling a skirt to the ladies.

Calls out who, tells you why, and includes the word new to get them interested.

“For sale at…266, 312, and 314 Fulton Street.”

The point of these is really just to get you into their doors.

Just a landing page click.

The offer and variants can sell you after.

They get you into the door by making you feel as if you are missing out on something.

By being warned with rather aggressive messaging.

Simple stuff.

But something that can be used even today.

Of course, get creative with it if you want it to work.

The messaging is quite old.

In conclusion:

If this was as painful for you to read as it was for me to type…

…then thank you for sharing in my pain.

As this was rather painful.

Mentally foremost.

Hip-wise second.

As I have been sitting all day and feel like shite.

But if there’s one thing I don’t skip, it's the gym.

I did a very intensive, but quick, back and bicep workout.

Then I did sprints at night and in the middle of the street till I felt worn out.

To be honest, it was only like 5 full on dashes.

But I hit it hard.

I just want to make something very clear to all of you.

At the end of this 90 days, I don't know where I'll be.

But this isn't just about the posts.

I plan on breaking down my body and soul.

To find my true limits as an individual.

And become the best version of myself.

For everyone that I care about in my life.

So, thank you for watching that happen.

1/6th of the way through the posts.

But just the start of this new life.

Now…

…for those of you who are learning copywriting, while also being new to this world.

I highly recommend two things!

1. Do the same as I, handwrite old sales letters and work on learning just as much as writing.

AND

2. Join @TheCopyTitan Svet Dimitrov's Skool for copywriting. 

They are an extremely pleasant bunch, and I see it growing to become much larger in due time.

I really cannot recommend this guy enough.

If you’d like to see all the recorded masterclasses…

…as well as Svets weekly copy breakdowns.

My affiliate link to his wonderful community is in my bio.

Please do take a peek.

Now.

To end in similar fashion...

Please feel free to point out where I'm wrong.

Where I'm Mistaken. 

OR 

Perhaps even where I'm right.

Although I do learn the most, in knowing what I did wrong.

Thank you for reading this!

Most people think using Claude Code is about writing better prompts.

It’s not.

The real unlock is structuring your repository so Claude can think like an engineer.

If your repo is messy, Claude behaves like a chatbot.

If your repo is structured, Claude behaves like a developer living inside your codebase.

Your project only needs 4 things:

• the why → what the system does
• the map → where things live
• the rules → what’s allowed / forbidden
• the workflows → how work gets done

I call this:

The Anatomy of a Claude Code Project 👇

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

1️⃣ CLAUDE.md = Repo Memory (Keep it Short)

This file is the north star for Claude.

Not a massive document.

Just three things:

• Purpose → why the system exists
• Repo map → how the project is structured
• Rules + commands → how Claude should operate

If CLAUDE.md becomes too long, the model starts missing critical signals.

Clarity beats size.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

2️⃣ .claude/skills/ = Reusable Expert Modes

Stop repeating instructions in prompts.

Turn common workflows into reusable skills.

Examples:

• code review checklist
• refactoring playbook
• debugging workflow
• release procedures

Now Claude can switch into specialized modes instantly.

Result:

More consistent outputs across sessions and teammates.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

3️⃣ .claude/hooks/ = Guardrails

Models forget.

Hooks don’t.

Use hooks for things that must always happen automatically.

Examples:

• run formatters after edits
• trigger tests after core changes
• block sensitive directories (auth, billing, migrations)

Hooks turn AI workflows into reliable engineering systems.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

4️⃣ docs/ = Progressive Context

Don’t overload prompts with information.

Instead, let Claude navigate your documentation.

Examples:

• architecture overview
• ADRs (engineering decisions)
• operational runbooks

Claude doesn’t need everything in memory.

It just needs to know where truth lives.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

5️⃣ Local CLAUDE.md for Critical Modules

Some areas of your system have hidden complexity.

Add local context files there.

Example:

src/auth/CLAUDE.md
src/persistence/CLAUDE.md
infra/CLAUDE.md

Now Claude understands the danger zones exactly when it works in them.

This dramatically reduces mistakes.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Here’s the shift most people miss:

Prompting is temporary.

Structure is permanent.

Once your repository is designed for AI:

Claude stops acting like a chatbot...

…and starts behaving like a project-native engineer. 🚀

Follow @swadeshkumar_ for more !!

There’s rarely a straightforward path to closing a deal. People go quiet. New people show up. Requirements change.

2102446829530968078.text:
Jev clearly explained (and how to make money with it):

The 80/20: keep your frontier LLM as the brain and swap in Jev as the hands. Jev doesn't write text. It picks from multiple choice options you define, much faster  (and MUCH cheaper) than an LLM. 

@nickvasiles is the co-founder of Orgo, and he came on the pod to break down what JEV actually is and where it makes you money. Here's what I learned:

1. Jev is not an LLM. It's a decision maker. You give it the question and choices A, B, C, D, and it answers with a confidence score. It can't output text at all.

2. It's a money-saving model, not a money-making model. If you're running an AI offer at 0% or 50% margin today, Jev can push that to 90 to 99%.

3. His proof: a computer use agent that scraped 60 products into a Zoho CRM cost $30/hour and ran 2 to 3 hours per batch. Rebuilt on JEV, he estimates under 10 seconds for practically free.

4. It played Minecraft for six pennies. Full computer use, tools defined by GPT-6 Astra, executed by Jev.

5. The "look now" detector: 16 Orgo computers watching X in real time, 4 criteria, Jev fires an alert when a model release matches 3 of 4. Same job on a frontier model would cost hundreds of dollars a day.

6. The architecture is GPT-6 as the brain, Jev as the execution layer. That's the harness Orgo is building around it for computer use.

7. Where it fits: high volume, structured inputs. Insurance claims by the thousand. Monitoring every skincare brand in your category for price drops. Online arbitrage scanning Kohls and Ulta for pennies.

8. On its own it's dumb. He asked it to play chess and it made exactly one move, instantly, then stopped. You have to build its brain out before it can act.

9. If you're not already making money with AI, Jev is a distraction. Go build an agent that's really good at one workflow for one customer first.

10. Ask your existing agent to figure it out. His Hermes agent Dewey studied the Jev docs, integrated the API, and built the demos himself.

His 2 key takeaways:

1. Bet on cost going to zero. He sold $5K/month managed agents with unlimited tokens at break-even because model costs only move one direction. Jev is that bet paying off.

2. Don't get FOMO. It's already been open sourced and the big labs will package it into the products you already use. Build the workflow now, swap the engine later.

Nick is building at the edge of computer use and we had a blast going deep on it. Go follow @nickvasiles

Here's how to execute this system at scale: 

1. point your agent at your cold email sequencers API docs - typically they will have a new reply webhook. 

2. Feed new reply webhook directly into Jev to classify the reply as interested or disinterested.

3. A: A second jev layer sorts disinterested as angry or not angry (honest objections for instance) 

angry people get a reply offering them to unsub from a database like apollo 

Objections get passed to grok bot. 

B: The second jev layer on the positive side sorts and tags by: referral, pricing questions, meeting request, question

4. you run this classification into a slack channel so you can see replies as they come in. 

Grok montitors that slack channel and is pinged when a reply comes through 

make sure he knows to prioritize positive replies. 

5. grok handles the response, you approve drafts -> each approval becomes training data for grok to improve his skills on.

6. you give grok access to the cal Api or log in to your calendar + CRM plugin so he can update the CRM and book calls. 

7. You set a routine to review reply work week over week and compare booking rates + start on new experiments like humor in responses, or just booking a time that makes sense for leads that never got back but expressed interest in a call. 

That's basically it. Feed this post to your grokbot.

2102672414320554355.text:
Robots have perfected physical movement, but they still struggle with context.

A robot can balance, walk, and navigate, but put it inside an unfamiliar warehouse where shelves move, new obstacles appear, and existing maps are instantly outdated and it struggles to function effectively.

That is the exact spatial intelligence gap @vangrid_io is working to solve.

Instead of relying on expensive, dedicated mapping vehicles that can't stay updated, Vangrid turns everyday smartphones into a crowdsourced visual network for autonomous systems.

Here is how the infrastructure works:

• On Ground Captures: Everyday users record real world locations city streets, office spaces, or active industrial facilities using standard mobile phones.

• On Device Privacy: Sensitive details like faces and license plates are processed and blurred directly on the device before anything gets uploaded.

• Data Verification: Every record carries a timestamp, approximate location, and digital fingerprint so robotics teams can verify exactly when and where the footage was taken.

• Targeted Bounties: Robotics companies needing coverage in a specific area can post monetary bounties to incentivize local captures.

For robotics teams, spatial data relies on three core principles:

1. Freshness: Maps must reflect real time conditions, not last year's layout.

2. Verification: Data sources must be authentic and tamper proof.

3. Privacy: Captures must respect individuals in public spaces.

The ultimate test for Vangrid will be coverage density and data consistency. 

If they succeed, smartphones won't just record the physical world they'll become the primary data pipeline powering autonomous machines.
